ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Block Control
ResponsesInList.Text: In fact, full screen isn't necessarily the best design either, and in fact, sometimes I wish Moodle took up less screen real estate and had more "white space" around text. Best practice is to have lines of text of approximately 9-10 words, so as to reduce people's need to move their eyes back and forth. I'd rather see more side blocks rather than less, as they would force the main content of the page to be less strung across the page. Same problem with long pages, requires people to scroll too much. That's why I'm a big fan of the book module concept. It simply offers better page design.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Block Control
ResponsesInList.Text: Erm ... firstly, the width decision is in your hands: make your window smaller ... Many people don't have that choice: try using a complex block-ridden site on a 640x480 browser for a while and you will see why Moodle generally makes the most of the page width.  In future some sort of user option like the one at the top of this discussion would be a good idea, but in the meantime full-width is better overall. And chunking long tracts of text into short ones is not always better page design , sometimes it's restrictive and frustrating. I'm guessing you don't have a scroll wheel on your mouse.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Block Control
ResponsesInList.Text: I have looked at Moodle on smaller screens. It works well on them. But personally I would rather see a site optimized for a smaller size screen that would expand the "white space" on bigger size screens rather than expand the text. The decision may be in the user's hand, but that doesn't mean they always make the best decision because they may not even realize what is best. And if you work with image rich pages as I do you have to factor that into the equation, and that affects page load time, layouts etc. It's just my philosophy, but I believe a good Web site is one in which enough thought is put into these issues that the design is such that there is no need to give users control over their environment. Usability is the responsibility of the designers, not the user.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Block title capitalization
ResponsesInList.Text: The salient difference here should be between title case and sentence case.  The former capitalizes all major words, but not short words like prepositions, the latter only capitalizes the first letter of the first word. I would prefer title case, however I think we only have a choice between sentence case and capitalizing every word without exception, Which Is Not Good Typography And Looks A Bit Strange On The Page. Tim.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Block title capitalization
ResponsesInList.Text: I just pulled the latest edition of the Chicago Manual of Style off the shelf to see what they have to say on this matter. They don't talk about Web sites, but they do talk about table headings, which are similar. There seems to be no hard and fast rule about which to use. However, in their general section on titles, they say that "Sentence style" is preferable when you have a very long title, but that "Headline Style" is often preferred for various reasons, including aesthetics (of course with the exceptions of prepositions and other short words). Considering that we are not talking about long strings of text like Timothy's example, I think that the latter seems more appropriate in this case.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Block title capitalization

ResponsesInList.Title: Course Formats and Default Blocks
ResponsesInList.Text: The block system currently has functionality built in to allow default blocks to be defined for specific course formats. Unfortunately, it is limited to the standard 'social' format and one default setting set in the config file. I propose that we allow a default block setting to be defined for any course format (standard and custom). I think the easiest way to do this would be to add an optional 'config.php' file in every course format directory. For blocks, this would mean that the course  'edit.php' file could pass any default blocks configuration string to 'blocks_get_default_blocks' instead of just depending on the site default. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: New Course Formats and Blocks
ResponsesInList.Text: Sorry Jon. I don't think I explained it well. There are two issues with creating a new course format. The first is that any new course format won't be accepted by the standard 'applicable_formats' call, because it is unknown. My first proposal dealt with this by assigning a catch-all format called COURSE_FORMAT_ALL as the default for the 'applicable_formats' method. This meant, that if a block did not specifically restrict a course format, it could be used by any course format and not just the standard ones. The next problem is that the 'course/view.php' function assigns specific bit values to the three standard formats, but won't recognize any other course formats. I solved this by defaulting any unknown course formats to the COURSE_FORMAT_ALL code. While this allows any new course format to access any block (the desired affect), it removes the ability for a block to restrict itself if necessary. An example would be the 'social_activities' block which really is only applicable to the social format. If we used a list of format names for the applicable course formats, and included 'course_format_all', 'course/view.php' would not have to know all of the possible formats. They would be provided by the blocks themselves as necessary. This would mean redoing the code for blocks that have already provided an 'applicable_formats' method however. So, what I'm trying to do is allow blocks to be available to all custom course formats, and still allow blocks to be selective if necessary. Blocks that have no reason to be selective should either return 'course_format_all' or simply not implement the method. Make sense? mike

For example, a block can be defined as a 'list_type' which already has some specific code constraints (it requires content and icon arrays, and an optional footer string). Why don't we create classes for these as well? I've attached an example of a 'list_type' class. These would fo right into the existing 'moodleblock.class.php' file rather than a separate file like this. Further, when we define a block with 'list_type', it should do the creation of this class for the block. So, add a constructor to the moodleblock class that takes a type as an argument and loads the appropriate type class. Thoughts? mike

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Block Type Classes
ResponsesInList.Text: Thoughts on this, in cryptographic-strength random order (it's 2 am over here... ): 1. Sure, I 'm all for this too. It didn't happen in the past because of the "must....release...." situation with 1.3, but now is the time for fresh initiatives! 2. Also, a minor issue in your code, Mike. In remove_item(), array_search() returns NULL (not false) when the item is not found for PHP < 4.2.0. Since Moodle requires PHP 4.1.0, this case has to be accounted for (I remember coding similar ugliness in Moodle recently, but not exactly where ). 3. If this is to happen, I propose a further change. First hint: I remember Martin commenting on "how many places you have to write the block name in in the blockfile when creating a new block". One of these places is the constructor. Second hint: at some point (don't remember when exactly) I added block_instance() in blocklib.php, which works like an "object factory": you tell it what object you want it to create, and it takes care of all the dirty work. Since block_instance() does all kinds of neat stuff like including required files etc, manually constructing block objects should now be prohibited on pain of death by the chinese water torture. The grand spoiler: lose the constructor entirely, and just have a construct() method. 4. The above is related to Mike's suggestion "add a constructor to the moodleblock class that takes a type as an argument and loads the appropriate type class". I don't fully understand what you mean Mike, but here are some thoughts: In all scenarios I can think of, the aim is to get the constructor of a class in the hierarchy called. This can be done in three ways: directly creating a specialized object with chained constructors, dynamically creating an object of a target class, and aggregating methods and properties to an existing object. Aggregating is out: object aggregation is experimental in PHP, and one time I tried it I got burned (there were bugs in PHP), so that one's out. Dynamically creating objects needs an object factory. You cannot make an object factory using the factory class' constructor, because in that case you would be creating a factory object each time (to run the constructor). You need a method instead, either a normal method of a singleton object (like $CFG) or a "static" method (one which doesn't use $this and can thus be called without creating an object) of a class. The latter option, which is used in DMS, is nothing more than a function protected from name conflicts by the "namespace" of the class it is derived in. The difference between Widget::create($type) and create_widget($type) is rather academic... Also, since I advocate the use of block_instance(), for dynamic object creation you would need to get the "block type" information from the block class itself. If that path is followed, it seems obvious to have something like function method() {return BLOCK_TYPE_LIST;} and have block_instance() get the return value by calling block_method_result(). If you don't have the acquiantance of these two ladies, take a look in blocklib.php. Chaining constructors sounds nice, but you have to do it manually: each class must have a construct() method, and each class' constructor must call parent::construct(). This ensures that your constructor chain will not break if you later move or add classes in your hierarchy, and the technique is also used in the DMS. PHP5 does away with the whole mess by providing magic constructors in the form of __construct(), but we cannot use PHP5 constructs in Moodle.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Block Type Classes
ResponsesInList.Text: Oh... I didn't get you in the first round and went a bit off topic then! OK then, my thoughts on this: Hmmm... basically what you 're saying is that each block should handle its content "internally" (i.e., use methods to "hide" the content representation from the programmer). This means that the block will also have to display itself, because hiding the content representation from the programmer is no good if display the block using a function which, well, needs access to that same representation! (print_side_block() or something like that, it's in the code). However, making blocks display themselves is bad, very bad, because we 'll be getting UI code in the block classes. All my instincts scream against doing this. There is a solution, of course. The elegant thing would be to create a "UI handler" object, which would be responsible for displaying ANYTHING on screen. Let me connect this idea with Martin's templates and improvise a bit: 1. The block is created. Content is added to it using appropriate methods that it exposes. 2. The time comes to display the block. Let's assume we have a "UI handler" object, which we will conveniently refer to as $UI. 3. Call $UI->display($block_object). Now, $UI will need to do a little sniffing so as to decide what to do with the block object. 4. Did I tell you that ALL the block classes, and all other visual elements, will need to be derived from a class like UI_object? 5. $UI sees that $block_object is derived from UI_object. It is thus assured that $block_object will provide any methods needed to expose its content. For example, let's call $block_object->get_display_stuff() and get the results. get_display_stuff() is defined in class UI_object and overridden in all derived classes (chaining up to the parent, of course). 6. We now have the $display_stuff. $UI knows what type of object $block_object is, and it knows the $display_stuff. It can then decide what to do to display it. For example, it can assign $display_stuff to $SMARTY template engine object variables and then call $SMARTY->display($template_file). The value $template_file will be deduced from the object's type. The above solution makes it extremely easy to convert between any display engine you want or will want in the future. It also completely disconnects UI elements from the HTML that will be used to display them. It hides the internal representation of their "content" from the programmer. It bells and it whistles. But the price is obvious... LOTS of work, a complexity increase that the current status of Moodle may not warrant. When designing the block system, making each block responsible for displaying itself would be an obvious feature to implement. But we didn't do it, exactly because of all the above. I hope it helps, one way or another. PS: Now that Greece have reached the Euro finals we 're "informally" celebrating all day here! Good thing, celebrating!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Block Type Classes
ResponsesInList.Text:
I'm assuming there is a display routine somewhere that looks for just
such a content object when the block is a list type. Why not formally
define it? Actually there isn't... rather, when we 're printing the blocks, and each block is queried for its content, it's also queried for its type. Then, some "legacy" (pre-blocks) function is called, with arguments according to the information we gathered. I agree with your very logical suggestion, take it in small steps. So here's my suggestion on this (I 'd do it myself but... time time time!): Create a trivial class hierarchy (let's plan for the future!) which could go something like this: UI_Element => UI_List => UI_IconList and UI_Element => UI_HTML. => denotes inheritance. Give each class a construct() method which just calls the constructor by name. This is necessary so that derived classes can successfully call the constructor chain without knowing the name of their parent class, using parent::construct(). Constructors should have no required arguments, as we might want to create an object of a class without any relevant data in hand. Give the classes methods much like the ones you describe. You can go a long way towards a Moodle-style friendly implementation here. For example, a UI_IconList is all good and well, but if for some reason we later change it to UI_SimpleList (which e.g. is just an HTML unordered list), we wouldn't want the code to break completely. So, the method add_icon() or something like that could be defined in UI_List and be empty. Obviously, each block creates a relevant object for its content, and the programmer adds to it using "wrapper" functions defined in the block (exactly as you describe). When the time comes to print the block, get_content() should return the whole UI_xxx object. You can then define a print_me() method in the UI_ classes and just do $content->print_me(). Later on we can always move this code around if needed. Jon

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Block Type Classes
ResponsesInList.Text: Jon - Here's a further developed example. In this example, I have rewritten the top-level MoodleBlock class, and created three new classes: MoodleBlockType: An interface class created only to fully define what a block type should look like. MoodleBlock_TextType: An implementation of MoodleBlockType for TextType blocks. MoodleBlock_ListType: An implementation of MoodleBlockType for ListType blocks. With this implementation, I have recreated the BlockType interfaces at the block level, so that specific Moodle Block implemetation don't need to know the specifics of the block types. They just need to know the common interface methods to call to load up their content. I have also included rewritten versions of the calendar month block (text type) and the site main menu block (list type), using the new class definitions, for review. This version of  'moodleblock.class.php' will still work with any existing block implementations (including the original calendar and main menu blocks). If we start with something like this, we can then change the implementations of the specific block types later, to use any UI classes that we define. What do you think? mike

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Block Type Classes
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Jon - Here's an example of what I mean. I have added the class MoodleBlock_ListType to the moodleblock.class.php file. This defines what a ListType block is, and provides some methods to use it. This makes it easier for a block developer to know what is required of a ListType. We would do the same with the other block types, and allow for a generic one. In this example, I have created a new block called bookmarks. To instantiate it, I just use the MoodleBlock constructor with the required information - name, course, blocktype and version. The specified type constructs the proper content object for me. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Block error in Administration section
ResponsesInList.Text: I tracked down the problem. I'm not sure why everyone hasn't had this problem yet. I will probably turn it in as a bug unless someone can prove that I'm crazy. I found that the error was originating from an error in the upgrade_blocks_plugins() function in blocklib.php. The function checks through the blocks listed in the /blocks directory. For each block it checks that certain methods (namely the constructor) in the block class is there. The errant code is: if( !in_array(strtolower($classname), $methods)) { //No constructor $notices[] = "Block $blockname: class does not have a constructor"; $invalidblocks[] = $blockname; continue; } The problem is the code lower cases the classname it checks for in the methods array, but the constructor names have upper case letters. So obviously, it doesn't "find" the constructor name in the array, and outputs the notice. Once I removed the strtolower() function, blocks were detected and added to the database (which it had never done previously as there were no blocks in the database). Hope this helps someone else. --Nicole

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Block error in Administration section
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Nicole, This error is caused by the object system change in PHP 5. In PHP5, functions that return class and method names return them case sensitive, changing the PHP4 behavior where they were always returned in lower case. To begin with, that's why you get these errors. Now, if you take the strtolower() call out of the check, the code will function just fine for you but will break for users of PHP 4 so that's no general solution either. The correct way would be to array_walk() the $methods array and make them all lowercase before the checks. I 'll put this in CVS in a few days (bit short of time right now). It's just that up to this point, with no official PHP5 out there is not much feedback to identify these issues. So thank you for reporting this! Regards, Jon

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: No blocks after updating from cvs in existing courses
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Greg, Now, you can follow this steps: Take a look to "mdl_config" table. It must have a record with name = "blocks_version" and value = "2004042700". It this isn't true, stop here!! Make a backup of your entire DB (using phpMyAdmin or shell commands) to be able to go back if necessary!! Execute this sql commands against your DB: update mdl_course set blockinfo = '' then: update mdl_course set blockinfo = '9,1,3,4,11,2,5:7,10' where format !='social' and blockinfo = '' and: update mdl_course set blockinfo = '9,11,3,4,13,10,2,5' where format = 'social' and blockinfo = '' This will update the blockinfo field to default values. Update your "moodle" dir with the latest files from CVS. If everything was ok, now every course in your server will have their default blocks configuration... I've tried it against my test server (with some different numbers) and it has worked fine!! Ciao PS: This trick is only valid for the blocks table content posted above by Greg and it will reset every course blocks configuration to their "default" status. ResponsesInList.Title: Modular blocks implementation progress
ResponsesInList.Text: I 'm posting Eloy's latest checklist of "need-to-do" items, so we can track the progress. Not coincidentally, starting a new forum thread in a more suitable place. The hide/show and delete options together seems a bit crazy for me. I think we should select one of them, isn't it? The add block should be used to add new blocks only (not to show hidden blocks). If all the right blocks are hidden or deleted then the add block is missing. If all the blocks in any side are hidden, then there is no way to show them again, perhaps "deleting" the TD should occur only when !isediting(). ResponsesInList.Title: Admininistering blocks
ResponsesInList.Text: There is something probably I'haven't very well understood in the blocks Administration->Coonfiguration->Blocks The "show hide" column shows the open eye icon: trying to hide the block, the icon does not change to closed eye nor the block disappear from the courses. When clicking on the open eye icon belonging to the "Social activities " block, all the open eyes icons change to closed eyes and all blocks hides from the courses layout. Clicking in the closed eye icon belonging to Social Activities does not allows the other blocks to reappear, it is needed to click on all the closed eye icon in the list before clicking in the icon belonging to Social activities. Where I'm wrong?

ResponsesInList.Title: Thanks for the Blocks!
ResponsesInList.Text: I recently obtained a CVS version of moodle and was pleasently surprised.  I've tuned out of the ongoing development of moodle and didn't know you all were so along with new concepts such as modular blocks.  I LOVE the fact that I can adjust the positioning of sideblocks within courses, as this opens new layout possibilities.  And I am looking forward to the implementation of blocks for the front page , as well as the never-ending march for new innovative blocks. Thank you all for your hard work.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Thanks for the Blocks!
ResponsesInList.Text: I agree with Chris. The development has moved on. Just within a couple of weeks being away, things have moved on. Again Thanks to all the people involved in making this the best it can be. Moodle "ROCKS"
